>[Crenshaw](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/7/7d/John%26SinaCrenshaw.jpg)â€™s kidnapping activities fit with what is known generally about kidnapping in Illinois. Turn of the century writer and historian Randall Parrish noted that the various laws concerning blacks in Illinois all but encouraged kidnapping:

>>The most odious feature of this entire slave code, however, was the kidnapping clause, which, unfortunately, had been so worded as to make capture and punishment for this crime almost impossible. The inevitable result in so new a country, overrun with desperate men, many of them criminally inclined, was to make such kidnapping of free negroes and indentured servants a regular and profitable business. They were seized everywhere by force, or inveigled by strategy upon river boats, and taken South into the cotton States, to be sold to the highest bidder. No crime can be greater or more revolting than this, yet for many years southern Illinois afforded a safe retreat to these kidnapping outlaws, who became more and more numerous and bold. In some instances they were organized into regular bands, having rendezvous and passwords, leaders, and methods of distributing the spoils of their nefarious trade in human suffering. The rough hill country lying between the Ohio and the Mississippi witnessed in those days much of crime and sorrow never to be recorded. Very few cases, indeed, ever found permanent mention.

______________

**tl;dr:**

Before and during the American Civil War, there was a booming trade in kidnapping free African Americans from the North, smuggling them South, and selling them as slaves. Once they were in a Southern state, nobody would believe that they were ever free in the first place.

These are based on a desire for non-corporate open software decentralized alternatives (if you're looking for a right-leaning user community, you probably won't find it there...), but sadly, none have achieved a critical mass in user base, which is what most attracts users to a social platform. The Internet tends to favor the first example of a kind of service whose brand becomes definitive for it, even if it is functionally inferior to later competitors.
